Can a cancellation itself be undone (the appointment reinstated), and what happens if the slot was taken by someone else in the meantime? — A mis-click cancel is common. Whether the system offers 'restore', and whether it refuses because the slot is gone or bumps the new booking, are distinct behaviours with no default in the request.

When a client reschedules only one attribute (e.g. the time), does the system keep the previously chosen therapist and treatment, or force the client to re-select everything? — Defines what a partial change deliberately leaves alone. Keeping the rest may silently produce an invalid combination (therapist not working the new time); forcing re-selection is safer but more friction. Both are reasonable and behave differently.

When a session is shorter or longer than the treatment's standard block (client arrives late, leaves early, therapist ends early, or the session overruns), how is the actual time priced: full advertised price regardless, pro-rata per minute, or rounded up/down to the nearest duration tier? — The same appointment can produce three different invoice totals. Pro-rata favours the client on short sessions; block/round-up favours the centre. This is a stated policy with tax-invoice and consumer-law consequences, and staff and clients will observe different amounts charged for identical clock time.

In which direction, and to whose benefit, are derived money amounts rounded (percentage discounts, promo codes, tax added or extracted, loyalty credit, splitting one total across payment methods)? — Round-half-up, round-half-down, round-to-nearest-5-cents, and round-per-line vs round-on-total all yield different final charges and different tax remitted. The cent that appears or disappears is either the centre's gain or the client's, and it must reconcile against the payment processor and the tax return.

If a client cancels, is money already taken refunded in full, refunded partially, converted to non-refundable credit toward a future booking, or kept entirely — and how does this vary with how far ahead the cancellation is made? — Refund vs credit vs forfeit are distinct observable outcomes with different accounting entries and different chargeback/consumer-protection exposure. The notice thresholds (e.g. 24h, 48h) are arbitrary until chosen, and each choice changes what the client gets back.

If a client does not show up, is the amount already taken kept as a no-show fee, offered as credit, or refunded — and if kept, is it the full price or a capped fee? — A no-show can be treated as a completed sale, a partial penalty, or a wash. Each produces a different revenue figure, a different tax treatment, and a different dispute risk, and the client visibly either loses their money or does not.

At the moment of online booking, does the system charge the full treatment price, a deposit (and if so, what fraction, rounded how), or nothing until after the session — and is any deposit later applied to the balance, refundable, or forfeited on cancellation? — This determines how much money enters the centre's account before service is rendered, what liability it represents on the books, and what the client is owed if the booking falls through. A 'deposit' of 30% of an odd price also forces a rounding-direction choice.

When a booking is modified and the new price differs — client swaps to a cheaper or dearer treatment, reschedules into a differently priced slot, or the centre reassigns them to a therapist on a different rate — is the difference refunded, issued as credit, charged additionally, or simply absorbed, and does the answer depend on whether the client or the centre initiated the change? — A downgrade can hand the client cash, a credit, or nothing; an upgrade can trigger a second charge or be given away. Making it depend on who initiated the change is a fairness policy with real revenue impact, and each rule produces a visibly different balance owed or returned.

When a client asks to close/delete their account (or is deactivated for non-payment/abuse) while they have upcoming appointments, are those appointments cancelled first, is deletion blocked until after they pass, or do the appointments remain on the staff schedule with the client's identity retained, anonymised, or replaced by a placeholder? — This decides whether staff still see who is coming in, whether the slot is freed, and how personal-data erasure requests are reconciled with keeping an operational schedule and historical records.

Are therapists and treatments hard-deleted, soft-deleted (recoverable/reactivatable), or archived, and how are past bookings that reference a now-removed therapist or treatment displayed in the day schedule, history and any reporting? — Historical appointments point at these records. Hard deletion breaks past-schedule views and revenue history; soft delete vs. archive determines whether a returning therapist's old data reconnects and whether removed treatments still render correctly in past-day views.

If deactivating a therapist leaves a treatment with no qualified provider, does the system automatically hide that treatment from online booking, leave it bookable with no assignable therapist, or flag it for an admin to resolve? — The treatment offering effectively has no owner once its sole provider departs. Leaving it bookable lets clients reserve appointments no one can perform; auto-hiding silently reduces the visible menu; each is observably different for clients and staff.

If the selected treatment's duration runs past the therapist's shift end or the centre's closing time (or into a scheduled break), is the booking blocked, allowed with overrun, or is the slot simply never offered? — The last bookable start time depends entirely on this. A 90-minute treatment with 60 minutes left before closing either disappears from the list, is rejected on submit, or is accepted and creates unpaid overtime.

When the same real-world appointment is entered by two routes - the client books online and staff also enter it by phone, or staff enter it twice - does the system detect that this client already has an appointment at or near that time and warn, merge, or block, or does it create two independent appointments? — The two routes cannot both occupy the identical slot, so one path is a visible conflict error to staff or client; but near-miss times (3:00 and 3:15, or the same treatment twice that day) create two appointments that both consume capacity and both generate reminders. Whether the system flags the apparent duplicate changes what staff see on the day schedule and how many slots are consumed.
